questions.problem: Consider the scalar field $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y.$ Calculate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is any smooth path from $(-3,1)$ to $(1,-2)$ in ${R}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

In our case, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path $C$ are $A(-3,1)$ and $B(1,-2).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(1,-2)-f(-3,1) \\  & =(1)^{2}(-2)-(-3)^{2}(1) \\  & =-2-9 \\  & =-11.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that

$$

questions.problem: Consider the scalar field $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡y-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Calculate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is any smooth path from $(-\pi ,0)$ to $(0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ in ${R}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

In our case, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path $C$ are $A(-\pi ,0)$ and $B(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(0,\frac{\pi }{2})-f(-\pi ,0) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =(1-1)-(0+1) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Consider the scalar field $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+1}.$ Calculate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is any smooth path from $(-2,1)$ to $(0,3)$ in ${R}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

In our case, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path $C$ are $A(-2,1)$ and $B(0,3).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(0,3)-f(-2,1) \\  & =\frac{3}{{0}^{2}+1}-\frac{1}{(-2)^{2}+1} \\  & =3-\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{14}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=({y}^{2}-2x)\,i+2xy\,j.$ Calculate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is any smooth path from $(0,1)$ to $(1,3)$ in ${R}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

In our case, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path $C$ are $A(0,1)$ and $B(1,3).$

Notice that $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ with domain $D={R}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2y.
$$

Since the partial derivatives exist and are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative. Therefore, we know there exists a function $f$ such that $∇f=F.$

Reconstructing $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f=x{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(1,3)-f(0,1) \\  & =(1(3)^{2}-{1}^{2})-(0(1)^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =8-0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$
